section.title: Introduction and Overview
section.p:
Usage of the Choices: structure has historically been disorganised, with each application author selecting their own particular way of storing options. Many applications fail to use the
way of accessing the Choices: structure, and some still use files kept in their own private directory structure.
This suggests the need for a central module to maintain configuration options for applications. The files it controls are textual, so as to allow the user to fix problems by hand if necessary.

item.p: A means of reading options files, either from Choices: or an arbitrary location
A means of writing options files, to the correct part of Choices: or to the original location
A means of collating related items within a file into 'groups'

subsection.title: User interface
subsection.p: There is no user interface provided by this module.

subsection.title: Programmer interface
subsection.p: The programmer interface is incomplete and may change without notice.

subsection.title: Data formats
subsection.p: Options files are standard RISC OS text files. Any whitespace (space or tab) at the beginning or end of a line is ignored. Any line where the first non-whitespace character is # is a comment line and is ignored, as is any line consisting only of whitespace.
The file consists of a series of groups, delimited by group name specifiers. A group name specifier starts with [, followed by the name (which may contain spaces), followed by ].
The groups themselves are in one of two formats (although further formats may be added in future):

item.p: The list format is a simple list of newline-terminated strings.
The options format consists of tag, value pairs in the form <spaces>tag name<spaces>:<spaces>value<spaces>, where <spaces> is zero or more spaces or tabs.

subsection.p: Items at the start of a file, before any group is declared, are deemed to be in the group $. Group names are case insensitive, as are tag entries.

p.extended-example:
An example options file for an application called "widget"
# choices file for widget
[auto load] # a list of files to load when starting widget ADFS::4.$.afile ADFS::4.$.somedir.anotherfile ADFS::4.$.thingy
[misc options] somevalue : 42 window width : 332 auto open : Yes

subsection.p: When a group is read with or written with , its content is passed as a block of memory in one of two layouts, matching the group format.
For an options group, the block holds a series of tag/value pointer pairs, terminated by a null pair:

offset-table.offset: Pointer to value 0, or NULL if no value is set (for example in list groups)

subsection.p: For a list format group, the buffer is filled with a series of null-terminated strings immediately following one another.

subsection.title: External dependencies
subsection.p: This specification has no external dependencies.

section.title: SWI calls
section.p: This module allocates the Options_ SWI chunk at &hex;52F80.

entry.register-use:
Flags:
R1 contains an absolute filename R1 contains the leafname, R2 contains the application name, and R3 contains another directory name to use if Choices: is not present, or the Choices: file is not present Reserved
Reserved, must be 0

use.p: This SWI is used to open a specific file, or a Choices: file, for access. When opening a specific file (type 0), only that file is written to and read from.

When opening a Choices: file (type 1), the file read comes from Choices:<application>.<leafname> if that is present, or if not, from <directory>.<leafname>. This provides compatibility for applications written for older systems. When writing, data is written to <Choices$Write>.<application>.<leafname> unless the Choices: structure is not present, in which case it is written to <directory>.<leafname>.

swi-definition.name: Options_CloseFile
swi-definition.description: Close a file, writing out any changes that are pending

use.p: This SWI is used to close an Options file session. Any changes are written out to the relevant file. An error may be produced if the options file could not be written.

swi-definition.name: Options_ReadGroup
swi-definition.description: Reads in a group description block to produce a value/tag array

entry.register-use:
Flags:
Options format List format
Other values are reserved.
Reserved, must be 0
Length of buffer, or negative to return the size of buffer needed

exit.register-use: Size of data written, or negative size of buffer needed

use.p: This SWI is used to read a group structure into a block of memory. The block is in one of the two formats described in Data formats, depending on the group type requested.

swi-definition.name: Options_WriteGroup
swi-definition.description: Writes a group description block to the options file

entry.register-use:
Flags:
Options format List format
Other values are reserved.
Reserved

use.p: This SWI is used to write data from a description block to a file. The contents of the buffer should be in the same format as for . The group type must match that of the group being written to, otherwise an error is generated.

swi-definition.name: Options_ReadValue
swi-definition.description: Reads the value of a single options tag

entry.register-use:
Flags:
Options format List format
Other values are reserved.
Reserved

exit.register-use: Pointer to a null terminated string containing the value for the tag

use.p: This SWI is used to read the value of a single option. The returned string should be considered read only.

swi-definition.name: Options_WriteValue
swi-definition.description: Writes the value of a single options tag

entry.register-use:
Flags:
Options format List format
Other values are reserved.
Reserved
Pointer to tag name, or line number for list format

use.p: This SWI is used to write the value of a single option.

swi-definition.name: Options_DeleteValue
swi-definition.description: Removes an option from a group

entry.register-use:
Flags:
Options format List format
Other values are reserved.
Reserved
Pointer to tag name, or line number for list format

use.p: This SWI is used to remove a single option.

swi-definition.name: Options_ReadBoolean
swi-definition.description: Converts a string into a boolean value

use.p: This SWI converts a string into a boolean value.
The strings are converted as follows, ignoring case: true, yes, on, and 1 are converted to TRUE (1). The strings 0, no, off, and false are converted to FALSE (0).

swi-definition.name: Options_ReadEnum
swi-definition.description: Converts a string into an integer value

entry.register-use: Pointer to a comma separated list of strings

exit.register-use: The index into the array that matches the given string, or -1 if it does not match any of them

use.p: This SWI converts a string into an index value. The string being matched can contain any character except control characters and a comma. The strings are matched case insensitively.

subsection.title: Acceptance test
subsection.p: The options file parser must be capable of coping with very malformed files. Users, and programmers, will edit the files by hand and often get that wrong. At worst the program should fail to read a few options, but even in the worst cases the vast majority of the file should be able to be read.

The layout of option files must be preserved, as it will be laid out in such a way as to make it easier for the human reader. So, any whitespace must remain in the file after it is modified, as should any comments. If no changes are made to the options then the file written out should be identical to the file read in.
Transition to the Options system should be as painless as possible for both programmers and users.

subsection.title: Test strategy
subsection.p: The Options module should be tested by a number of programmers, in their own applications, as well as in some of the OS components.

section.title: Outstanding issues
section.p: The implementation of the read and write single value SWIs has to be worked on, but the whole file could be parsed when it is first opened. That way the values would already be in memory, so direct pointers could be returned.
